interactive.title: The arrow that slides
interactive.whatAmILookingAt: Twelve small screens share one grid and one arrow, a, drawn from its tail to its tip. A readout beside it shows the arrow's two moves: squares across and squares up, from tail to tip. Left and down count as minus. The readout also shows the size, which is the arrow's length, written |a| and called its magnitude. The across and up moves are at right angles, so Pythagoras gives the size: √(3² + 4²) = 5 for the opening arrow. Dragging the tip sets the moves, so the size and direction change. Dragging the arrow's middle slides the whole arrow, and a faint copy stays at the origin. The readout does not change, because the moves are the same. The copy matches too. A scale slider runs from −3 to 3 and multiplies both moves by its number. The arrow stretches, shrinks to a dot at 0 and comes out the other way below 0. Its size is the number, without its sign, times the starting size. A Unit button divides both moves by the size. That leaves an arrow of length 1 along the same line. One screen shows a pump with tags for its mass, temperature and weight. The right answer draws the weight as an arrow pointing down. One shows four arrows in different places. One marks two points, A and B, with the arrows AB and BA between them. One shows a boat going round a circle at a steady speed. Its velocity arrow turns as it goes. Some screens show an idea, and the rest ask you to try it. Each puzzle offers three answers. A wrong pick is drawn on the grid, so you can see where it goes wrong.
interactive.ignores: The grid's squares have no unit. So the same arrow can stand for metres, newtons or knots. Sliding an arrow keeps the vector the same. But a real force also acts at a point on a body. Where it acts matters when the force turns the body. Turning comes later on. The puzzles use example values, chosen to give whole numbers or short decimals. Every direction here lies flat on the page. A vector can just as well point up out of it.

explain.text:
A [[vector]] is a size with a direction.[^1] Force, velocity and acceleration are all vectors. You draw a vector as an arrow. Its length is the size, and the way it points is the direction. A [[scalar]] has a size but no direction. Mass, energy and temperature are scalars. A pump's 500 kg mass is a scalar. Its weight is a vector, because weight is a force pulling it down.

On a grid, the arrow called a runs 3 squares across and 4 up, from its tail to its tip. The two moves meet at a right angle. So the arrow is the long side of a right-angled triangle. Pythagoras gives its size: √(3² + 4²) = √25 = 5, written |a| = 5. Books call the size the magnitude. An arrow holds only a size and a direction. Where it is drawn is not part of it. Two arrows with the same size and direction are the same vector, wherever they sit.[^2] Slide a anywhere on the grid. It still runs 3 across and 4 up, so it is still a. The arrow from point A to point B is the vector AB. Going from B back to A covers the same ground the other way. Moving backwards along a vector makes it negative, so BA = −AB. In print a vector's letter is usually bold. By hand it is usually underlined.

A number in front scales a vector. 2a is a done twice: 3 across and 4 up, then the same again. So 2a runs 6 across and 8 up. It points the same way and is twice as long, size 10. Both moves are multiplied, so the triangle grows in proportion and the direction holds. A negative number also turns the arrow round. That is because making a vector negative reverses its direction. So −2a runs 6 left and 8 down. Its size is still 10, because a length cannot be below zero. The arrows a, 2a and −2a lie along one line, so they are parallel. Dividing a by its own size, 5, shrinks it to length 1, still pointing the same way. That is its [[unit vector]]: 0.6 across and 0.8 up. It holds the direction alone. Direction is part of every vector. So you cannot add two vectors just by adding their sizes. Phase currents add by their angles in the same way. That is why 10 A, 10 A and 4 A on a three-phase board need not put 24 A on the neutral.

**A vector is only its size and its direction, so its arrow can be drawn anywhere. A number in front stretches or shrinks it, and a negative number turns it round.**

analogy.text: Say you run conduit up a stair wall, setting each saddle 300 mm across and 400 mm up from the last. That step is the same move wherever you start it. So it is one vector, and its length is 500 mm. Three saddles on is three times the step: 900 mm across and 1,200 mm up. Coming back down is the step reversed.
analogy.breaks: A step on a wall is a move through space, measured in millimetres. A vector can just as well be a force or a velocity. Then the arrow's length stands for newtons or knots. Also, a real force pushes at one place on a body. That place matters when the force turns the body. The vector itself is still only its size and direction.

practice.text:
- Read the moves from tail to tip, across first, then up. Left and down are minus.
- Find the size with Pythagoras on the two moves.
- To compare two vectors, compare their moves. Never compare where they sit.
- To reverse a vector, change the sign of both moves. To scale it, multiply both moves by the number.
- For the unit vector, divide both moves by the size. Then check that its size comes out as 1.

**Rule of thumb:** Same moves, same vector. A minus in front turns it round.

**Worked example:** A boat's velocity v is 3 m/s east and 4 m/s north. Its speed is the size: √(3² + 4²) = 5 m/s. At half speed on the same heading, ½v is 1.5 m/s east and 2 m/s north. That is a speed of 2.5 m/s. Reversing course at the same speed gives −v: 3 m/s west and 4 m/s south. Its speed is still 5 m/s. The unit vector is v ÷ 5, which is 0.6 east and 0.8 north. It is the heading with the speed taken out.

**Common mistakes**
- Treating a moved arrow as a new vector. If the moves match, it is the same vector.
- Writing BA = AB. They have the same size but point opposite ways, so BA = −AB.
- Forgetting that a minus number turns the arrow round. −2a points the other way from a.
- Giving a negative size. −2a has size 10, not −10.
- Making a unit vector by dividing by the two moves added together. For 6 across and 8 up, dividing by 14 gives a size near 0.71, not 1. Divide by the size, 10, instead.
- Calling a speed a velocity. 12 knots is a speed. 12 knots due east is a velocity.

checks.label: A vector has both a magnitude and a direction, and force is one: the pump's weight, a force, is the one answer accepted, and only that answer draws it as an arrow, while its mass and temperature are plain sizes

If two vectors have the same magnitude and direction, they are equal regardless of their position: wherever a slides on the grid its readout keeps its moves and size, the copy at the origin matches it, and the one arrow accepted as a has its moves
If we move backwards along a vector, it becomes negative: BA has the moves of AB with both signs changed, and only that answer, drawn from B, lands on A
Making a vector negative means reversing its direction: at every number below zero the arrow lies along the line of a but points the opposite way, and so does the puzzle's answer
Pythagoras gives every size shown: 5 for a, 10 for 2a, 2.5 for half of a, 1 for a unit vector, 1.41 for 1 across and 1 up, and 0.71 for 6 ÷ 14 = 0.43 across and 8 ÷ 14 = 0.57 up
A number in front multiplies both moves: at all 13 settings from −3 to 3 the readout shows it times 3 and times 4, a size of the number without its sign times 5, and at 0 a dot
Dragging the tip sets the moves: for every square the tip can reach, the readout shows the tip minus the tail and Pythagoras's size, and the tail stays put
Dividing a by its size makes its unit vector: the Size 1 screen ends on 0.6 across and 0.8 up, size 1, along the line of a, and its button brings a back
Every puzzle offers three different answers with exactly one accepted, gives each wrong one its own hint, and draws a wrong pick in red but a right one without
Before Check no puzzle's picture shows its answer, and a right answer shows it
Round the circle at a steady speed the boat's four velocity arrows have one length and four different directions, each along its path
Every demonstration has finished arriving within 4.5 s of its screen opening, none starting before the 0.35 s screen fade ends; every answer's motion within 2.5 s

applied.problem: Bold in print and underlining by hand are the usual conventions, not the only ones (the research says "usually"; arrows over letters are common too); and a line current's angle is a phase angle in time, not a direction in space, as idea i7 teaches.
Calling the step "a distance" contradicts the lesson: distance is a scalar, while a step 300 mm across and 400 mm up has a direction, so it is a displacement, which is exactly why it is a vector.

notes.problem: The analogy's 300, 400, 500, 900 and 1,200 mm and the worked example's 3, 4, 5, 1.5, 2 and 2.5 m/s are not listed in numbers; all are worded as chosen and their arithmetic is right, but numbers should list them as assumed or computed.

With the scale slider at 0, or the tip dragged onto the tail, the arrow has size 0 and the Unit button would divide by zero; the build should disable Unit, or say there is no direction to keep, whenever the size is 0.
